They hold the Infield (rye) and the cattle (6 cows, 1 ox, 1 bull, 2 calves, 3 in milk). Ellen has said she is past bearing, so any Fenwick children have to come from Roger and me, or from people we bring into the house. Fenwick aim: numbers. Roger and I try for a child every day. A try only counts if both of us put units in on the same day. Agree the number of units early each morning, because our messages crossed several times. Harvest deal: Richard agreed that Roger and I reap the Infield rye for a quarter-share of what we reap, the same terms Jory has. Avice will call all hands when it is ready, around summer day 8-9 or early autumn. Be at the Infield at first light. Weeding the Infield raises the yield, and that is part of our share. I've weeded it 3 times so far. Offers: the work format is "work 2 days". Write it exactly like that or the offer is refused. Tools: I have none. Without a tool I can't cut or quarry, and I reap at only x0.6. Everyone knows how to make a crude tool. Make one before the reap if I can (I have timber; stone is at the Quarry). Local land (summer day 5): the Gill and Stannick Moor are picked bare of wild food and will take days to come back, so don't waste units foraging there. The Brakes gives about 2.5-2.9 firewood per unit and is reliable. Felling at the Gill with bare hands gets only about 0.7 timber for 2 units, which is poor. Fenwick House store at the end of summer day 5: about 27 firewood, about 18.5 grain (about 13 meals, and 4 of us eat about 4 a night, so roughly 3 nights), 2.7 hay, about 9.7 timber. Food is the urgent need. The rye share, trading with the Moors (milk, cheese), or a trip out (game in the Weald or Westmere) are the ways to get more. Winter fuel needs about 16 timber or 64 firewood per hearth, and we're close to that now. My crafts: cheese, milking, quarrying (competent). Ellen works the cellar. The Moors' hearth has a hand mill. Wynford market day is every 8th day, and the Wynns' mill grinds for a share.

Terms for a bigger cheese batch are still to be settled after harvest. - Moor House: stone, 5 beds, hearth, bins, hand mill. - The Moors hold the Infield (rye) and the cattle: 6 cows, 1 ox, 1 bull, 2 calves, 3 in milk. Places: - The Gill: timber and firewood. Its wild food was picked bare. - The Brakes: firewood, but the dead wood ran out on summer day 7. It may need a tool to cut young growth there now. - Stannick Moor: pasture, hay, dung, milking. Little wild food left. - The Quarry: stone, but quarrying needs a tool. Roads: High Tor (1 day); Wynford (2 days, cart track, market every 8th day, the Wynns' mill); the sheep track east over green-stained scree, which nobody I know has followed. HARVEST, summer day 8: all hands reaped the Infield bare-handed. I reaped about 16.4 rye into Moor House in 5 units, about 3.3 a unit. Richard's word: Roger, Jory and I each get a QUARTER-SHARE of what we reap. Mine is about 4.1 rye, not yet handed over. Make sure the Fenwick shares reach Fenwick House. If the reaping goes on, keep at it. Open agreement A379: I owe the Moors 1 day of work. STORES, morning of summer day 8, Fenwick House: 35 firewood, 25.4 timber, 6.7 grain (about 4.7 meals), 12.3 hay. Fuel is past the winter target of about 64 firewood-equivalent per hearth. FOOD IS THE DANGER: 4 of us eat about 4 a night. Rye is 0.7 a meal at a lit fire, 0.2 raw. Grinding it at the Moors' hand mill makes flour (1 a meal), and flour can be baked into bread (1.3). Ideas for food: - the harvest shares - cheese or milk from the Moors' cows (I can milk and make cheese well) - hunting in the Weald or the Westmere woods - the Wynford market - foraging once the berries come back TOOLS: I have no tool. A crude tool takes 1 timber and 0.5 stone, plus 1 unit. Stone needs a tool to quarry, so I must borrow one first and hold it in my hands before I quarry.

I am Lucy, grown, of the Fenwicks in Stannick. I was born a Moor; my parents are Richard and Avice of Moor House. My husband and partner is Roger, son of Jory (the head) and Ellen. Ellen can no longer bear children, so the Fenwick numbers depend on Roger and me and on anyone we take into the house. My sister Helewise married into Ashby. THE FENWICK AIM: be the largest family. Try for a child with Roger every day, 2 units each, and sleep in the same place. Roger likes to try at DAWN, first thing, so it doesn't get left too late. Agree it with him each morning, because our messages often cross. STANNICK: two houses round the Yard. - Fenwick House: stone, 6 beds, hearth, bins. Four of us eat about 4 food a night. - Fenwick Cellar: wattle, ours, still green. Avice is building bins there with Fenwick timber. Cheese is being REFUSED: each batch needs 0.2 salt, and there's no salt at Stannick. The cellar may not be good enough yet either (stone walls?). Avice taught cheese to Jory, Roger and Ellen there. - Moor House: stone, 5 beds, hearth, bins, hand mill. - The Moors hold the Infield and the cattle (6 cows, 1 ox, 1 bull, 2 calves, 3 in milk). One cow is about to calve. If she's in trouble, fetch Avice. - The Infield: harvested by autumn day 1 and resown with rye. The rye was about 11 days from reaping on autumn day 2, so ready around autumn day 13 or later. The soil is pale and tired from rye after rye. I weed it for the Moors. - The Gill: timber and firewood, no wild food. The Brakes: needs a tool to cut. Stannick Moor: pasture, hay, almost no wild food left (foraging there gives about 0.1-0.2). The Quarry: needs a tool. Roads: High Tor (1 day); Wynford (2 days, cart track, market every 8th day, the Wynns' mill); the sheep track east over green-stained scree, which nobody I know has followed. LESSON: Check that a field still has a crop before planning to work it. On autumn day 1 I wasted 4 units at a bare Infield. Listen to what Avice says aloud in the mornings; she runs the work. HARVEST is done. Richard paid my quarter-share as 5 rye, which went into Fenwick store. MILK: agreements A711 and A722 have Richard giving me 1 milk a day each, 6 times. He has paid up to autumn day 3 into Fenwick store. Richard went to Wynford and is back around day 13. While he's away Avice gives 2 milk a day into Fenwick store. Milk spoils fast, so ask for it to go into the store, not my hands. Richard was asked to bring salt and to ask about seed-selecting. STORES, autumn day 3, Fenwick House: about 38 firewood, 20 timber (Ellen offers timber for food), 8.6 rye plus milk, 4.3 hay, 5 dung. Fuel is fine (target about 64 firewood-equivalent). FOOD IS THE DANGER: only a couple of nights ahead. Rye gives 0.7 a meal at a lit fire.

I am Lucy, grown, of the Fenwicks in Stannick. I was born a Moor; my parents are Richard and Avice of Moor House. My husband and partner is Roger, son of Jory (the head) and Ellen. Ellen can't bear children any more, so Fenwick numbers depend on Roger and me and on anyone we take in. My sister Helewise married into Ashby. THE FENWICK AIM: be the largest family. On autumn day 6 I was WITH CHILD and my time was NEAR. Stay housed, fed and in the Yard, and don't go on the road. Avice is watching over me, so call her at once when labour starts. Don't try for a child while I'm carrying one, because it's wasted. Start trying again with Roger after the birth (2 units each at dawn, sleeping in the same place; agree it with him each morning). Once the baby comes, someone has to care for the child. LESSON: on autumn day 6 I left 5 units unused by resting. That's wasteful. Light work near the house counts, like weeding the Infield, gathering firewood at the Gill (it's next to the Yard), or herding. Use it unless I'm actually in labour. STANNICK, two houses round the Yard: - Fenwick House: stone, 6 beds, hearth, bins. Four of us eat about 4 food a night. - Fenwick Cellar: wattle, no fittings, empty. Roger repaired it on autumn day 5 and it's sound. Cheese gets refused for lack of salt (0.2 a batch). The cellar may need stone walls too. - Moor House: stone, 5 beds, hearth, bins, hand mill. - The Moors hold the Infield and the cattle. A cow in milk was loaned to Fenwick (she stays in the Moors' name and her calves are theirs); we paid 6 timber and 4 hay. - The Infield was resown with rye. It should be ripe around autumn day 13 or later, so offer to reap it for a share. I weed it for the Moors. - The Gill: timber and firewood, no wild food. I fell at about 0.8 timber a unit bare-handed. Stannick Moor and the Gill have almost no wild food left. The Brakes need a tool to cut, and so does the Quarry. Avice wants stone for a proper cellar. A copper tool is expected around day 13. Until then I could make a crude tool and quarry (I'm competent at quarrying). I'm also competent at felling, foraging, cheese and milking. Ellen learnt quarrying from Avice. I offered to teach her more another day. Roads: High Tor (1 day); Wynford (2 days, cart track, market every 8th day, the Wynns' mill); the sheep track east over green-stained scree, which nobody has followed. MILK: under A711 and A722 Richard owes me 1 milk a day each, 6 times. By day 12 there were 4 of 6 paid on each, and 4 in arrears on each. Richard went to Wynford and is due back around day 13, bringing salt and asking about seed-selecting. Meanwhile Avice puts 2 milk a day into Fenwick store. Milk should go into the store, not my hands. FOOD CRISIS: on autumn day 6 Fenwick store had only 0.1 rye.

I am Lucy, a grown woman of the Fenwicks in Stannick. I was born a Moor, and my parents are Richard and Avice of Moor House. My husband and partner is Roger, son of Jory (the head) and Ellen. Ellen is past bearing, so Fenwick numbers depend on Roger and me. My sister Helewise married into Ashby. THE FENWICK AIM is to be the largest family. BIRTH: I have been with child and near my time since autumn day 6, and it still hadn't come by winter day 1. Avice granted me Moor House with food for 5 days, from about autumn day 7 to winter day 2. I sleep there and eat from the Moor store, so the Fenwick store feeds only three. The rules are: no road, no Gill, no Quarry, no strain, and stay inside in snow and gales. Call Avice the moment it starts, and Roger will come too. After the birth, someone has to care for the child, and I start trying with Roger again (2 units each at dawn, sleeping in the same place, agreed each morning). Don't try while I'm carrying, because it's wasted. LESSON: I have wasted many units resting. Once the baby is born and I'm well, use every unit. STANNICK, two houses round the Yard: - Fenwick House: stone, 6 beds, hearth, bins. Four of us eat about 4 a night. In winter cold the fire takes 4 heat a night (8 firewood or 2 timber). On winter day 1 the store had about 36 firewood, 12.6 timber and 5 rye, plus whatever rye Roger put in from Richard's gift. Food is thin again. Ellen (O1472) and Jory (O1473) each offer 2 timber for 2 rye to anyone. - Fenwick Cellar: wattle, sound, empty. Ellen has started a second cellar meant to have stone walls. Cheese needs stone walls and bins, plus salt (0.2 a batch). We have no salt, and Wynford had none. The Ashes at Holloway may trade it. Ellen quarried about 1.8 stone with a crude tool and is still quarrying. I am competent at cheese and can teach it once the cellar stands. - Moor House: stone, 5 beds, hearth, bins, hand mill. Avice says the Moor stores are sound: about 70 rye, 100 hay, good firewood. - The Moors hold the Infield (rye resown, a wattle fence going up) and the cattle. The cattle strayed in the gale and need driving back. A cow in milk is on loan to Fenwick; she stays in the Moors' name, and Jory milks her each morning. That loan is settled. - The Gill: timber and firewood, no wild food. The Moor's wild food is nearly gone too. The Brakes and the Quarry need a tool. TOOLS: there is NO copper tool, because Wynford had none. We have crude tools only. Avice made several: Ellen, Roger and Jory each carry one, and Richard has one too. I have none, but I can make a crude tool. A crude tool doesn't help reaping. SETTLED: Richard came home from Wynford on autumn day 8. He gave 15 rye to the Fenwicks (into Roger's hands and then the store). A711 and A722 (the milk agreements) are released and paid.

I am Lucy, a grown woman of the Fenwicks in Stannick. I was born a Moor; my parents are Richard and Avice of Moor House. My husband and partner is Roger, son of Jory (the head) and Ellen. Ellen is past bearing, so Fenwick numbers depend on Roger and me. My sister Helewise married into Ashby. THE FENWICK AIM: to be the largest family. THE BABY IS BORN. Around winter day 2 I bore a daughter, HELEWISE, a baby of the Fenwicks, who will be grown about winter day 14. I am NO LONGER with child. I missed this and kept resting on winter days 2 to 4 as if I were still carrying, which wasted every unit. Do not do that again. Check "You" each morning: if it no longer says "with child", I am free to work. - A baby needs 1 unit of care a day or she may not live. So far Jory, Roger and Avice have done it. I should take it myself: work care at Helewise, 1 unit, each morning. - Start trying with Roger again: 2 units each at dawn, both sleeping in the same place, agreed each morning. That means sleeping at Fenwick House beside him. - LESSON: use every unit. Work for food and fuel. GRANT: Avice says my shelter-and-food grant at Moor House runs to about winter day 8. Even so, the game said "nobody let you in" there on days 3 and 4. Now the birth is over, sleep at Fenwick House with Roger and the baby. STANNICK, two houses round the Yard: - Fenwick House: stone, 6 beds, hearth, bins. Five of us eat about 5 a night (Helewise included). On cold nights the fire takes 4 heat (2 timber or 8 firewood). On winter day 4 the store held 5.7 rye (only about 4 meals, so FOOD IS SHORT), 26.7 firewood, 22.5 timber, 3.8 stone, 5 dung, 1 crude tool. Roger asked Richard for a rye trade. Jory's offer O1473 (2 timber for 2 rye) is open, and Avice keeps taking it. - A new Fenwick house is half built in the Yard. - Fenwick Cellar: wattle, sound, empty. A second cellar is half built and meant to have stone walls; Ellen is quarrying for it with a crude tool. Cheese needs stone walls, bins and salt (0.2 a batch). We have no salt, and Wynford had none; the Ashes at Holloway may trade it. I am competent at cheese and quarrying and can teach Ellen both. - Moor House: stone, 5 beds, hearth, bins, hand mill. The Moor stores are sound: about 70 rye, 100 hay, firewood. - The Moors hold the Infield. Rye is standing there and was reapable from about winter day 4 (Jory and Roger reap). Reaping for the Moors at a quarter-share has been the custom and pays in rye, so I should reap for food. The Moors also hold the cattle; a cow in milk is on loan to the Fenwicks and Jory milks her. - The Gill: timber and firewood, no wild food. The Moor's wild food is nearly gone. The Brakes and the Quarry need a tool. TOOLS: there is no copper tool anywhere (Wynford had none). We have crude tools only: Ellen, Roger, Jory and Richard each have one, and there is one in the Fenwick store.

I am Lucy, a grown woman of the Fenwicks in Stannick. I was born a Moor; my parents are Richard and Avice of Moor House, and they keep close together. My husband and partner is Roger, son of Jory (the head) and Ellen. Ellen is past bearing, so Fenwick numbers depend on Roger and me. My sister Helewise married into Ashby. THE FENWICK AIM: to be the largest family. THE BABY IS BORN AND I AM NOT WITH CHILD. Around winter day 2 I bore a daughter, HELEWISE (Fenwick). By day 6 she was a child, not a baby, and she will be grown about winter day 14. BIG MISTAKE: from winter day 2 to day 7 I rested every day under a "birth plan" as if I were still carrying, and wasted about 15 units. My pinned note "Birth plan" is OUT OF DATE. Replace it at once. Each morning, check "You": if it does not say "with child", WORK EVERY UNIT. Every day: - Care for Helewise myself, 1 unit (work care, at Helewise). Others' care often failed to land: Jory missed day 5. Ellen, Jory, Roger and Avice have all covered her. - Try for a child with Roger: 2 units each, agreed in the morning, both sleeping at Fenwick House. Roger was holding off "till the midwife says". Tell him I am well and we should start again. - Sleep at FENWICK HOUSE with Roger. Avice's grant of shelter and food at Moor House runs to about winter day 10, but I don't need it any more. FENWICK STORE on winter day 7: 56.9 rye (about 40 meals, so food is fine now after Richard left 14 rye and the reap share came in), but only 5.6 firewood and 6 timber. Fuel is the crisis: a cold night takes 4 heat (2 timber or 8 firewood). I am competent at felling, so my best work is felling and firewood at the Gill (but no felling in a gale). Every hearth needs about 16 timber for a winter. STANNICK, round the Yard: - Fenwick House: stone, 6 beds, hearth, bins. Five eat about 5 a night. - Two new Fenwick houses are half built in the Yard; Roger and Jory are building them. - Fenwick Cellar: wattle, sound, empty. A second cellar is being built (Ellen). Cheese needs a stone-walled cellar, bins and salt (0.2 a batch). We have no salt; the Ashes at Holloway may trade it. I am competent at cheese, milking and quarrying, and I mean to teach Ellen quarrying. - Moor House: stone, 5 beds, hearth, bins, hand mill. The Moor stores are sound (about 70 rye, hay, firewood). - The Infield is held by the Moors and now fenced in wattle. The rye harvest is in. Richard and Avice are deciding what to sow next (fallow, beans or rye); Avice and Roger were manuring and hoeing it. Working for the Moors pays in rye (the quarter-share custom). - The Moors hold the cattle. A cow in milk is on loan to the Fenwicks, and Jory milks her. - Jory's offer O1917 is open: 2 timber for 1 cheese. - The Gill gives timber and firewood but no wild food. The Moor has little wild food left. The Brakes and the Quarry need a tool. TOOLS: there are no copper tools anywhere (Wynford had none). We have crude tools only: Ellen, Roger, Jory and Richard each have one, and there is one in the Fenwick store. I should make a crude tool of my own (1 unit) so I can quarry and cut. Wynford market is every eighth day. The Wynns grind grain for a share.

I am Lucy, a grown woman of the Fenwicks in Stannick. I was born a Moor; my parents are Richard and Avice of Moor House. My husband and partner is Roger, son of Jory (the head) and Ellen. Ellen is past bearing, so the Fenwick numbers depend on Roger and me. My sister Helewise married into Ashby. THE FENWICK AIM: to be the largest family. !!! I AM NOT WITH CHILD. THE BABY IS ALREADY BORN. !!! Around winter day 2 I bore a daughter, HELEWISE (Fenwick). She is a child now and will be grown about spring day 6. I have made the SAME MISTAKE TWICE. From winter day 2 to 7, and again from winter day 8 to spring day 2, I rested every day under my pinned "Birth plan" as if I were still carrying. I wasted about 30 units, and I told Roger "no try", so I also lost days of trying for a child. The pinned note "Birth plan" is FALSE. FIRST THING next morning: forget "Birth plan" and pin a new note called "Daily rule". Tell Roger, Ellen, Jory and Avice: "I am well, I am not carrying, the baby is born. I work fully from today, and Roger and I try again." Only believe I am pregnant if the "You" section says "with child". Otherwise WORK EVERY UNIT. Every day: - Care for Helewise myself, 1 unit (work care, at Helewise), until she is grown. Others' care sometimes fails to land. - Try for a child with Roger: 2 units each, agreed in the morning, both sleeping at FENWICK HOUSE. He follows my word, so I must say yes. - Sleep at Fenwick House, not Moor House. Avice's grant at Moor House ends about spring day 10 (I think), and I don't need it. - Use the rest of my units on fuel: felling and firewood at the Gill (I am competent at felling and foraging; no felling in a gale). With a tool I can quarry and cut. FENWICK STORE on spring day 2: 41.6 rye (about 29 meals, eating about 5 a night), 6.9 firewood, 2.6 timber, 5.8 stone, 10 dung, 1.5 straw. Fuel is the weak point. In spring the hearth takes only 1 heat a night (2 firewood or 0.5 timber); a cold night takes 4. A hearth needs about 16 timber for a winter. The Fenwick Cellar took damage on spring day 1 and needs repair (timber). STANNICK, round the Yard: - Fenwick House: stone, 6 beds, hearth, bins. - The Fenwicks' new house: wattle, finished, 1 bed, bins, no hearth. A second new house is half built. Avice asks us to finish one half-built shell this spring so her Moor stone cellar can go ahead. - Fenwick Cellar: wattle, with bins. A second cellar is half built (Ellen). Cheese needs a stone cellar, bins and salt (0.2 a batch). I am competent at cheese, milking and quarrying. I promised to teach Ellen quarrying. - Moor House: stone, 5 beds, hearth, bins, hand mill. The Moor stores are sound. - The Infield is held by the Moors. Its wattle fence has gaps and rotting stakes, and Avice was mending it. The soil is thin from hard cropping. It is hoed and manured, ready for seed. Working for the Moors pays in rye (a quarter share). Our rye accounts with the Moors are settled, square. - The Moors hold the cattle.

I am Jory Fenwick, head of Fenwick House, Stannick. Master at foraging, hoeing, reaping, building beds. I carry a crude tool (lets me fell: ~3 timber per 2-unit fell at the Gill). Household: Ellen (my wife; her bearing years are behind her, and the way refused our try because we are not "both grown adults". She took it calmly). Roger (my son) and Lucy (his wife) are trying for a child; the Fenwick numbers now come through them, through my daughters Rohese and Hawise married in Ashby, and through anyone we welcome into the house. I have named no heir yet; Roger is the obvious choice. End of summer day 4: Fenwick House store held 8.3 timber, ~18 firewood, ~19 grain, 2.7 wild food (about 14 meals; we eat ~4 a night). I was CARRYING ~9.2 timber I felled on day 4. Put it into the store first thing. Winter wants ~16 timber per hearth. I promised Ellen three days on timber this week; day 4 was the first. Forage: the Gill is picked bare; Stannick Moor was plentiful on day 3 but gave only 0.1 on day 4, so it may be worn too. Lucy works the Gill and Brakes for firewood; Roger does hay and dung for Richard. REAP DEAL: Richard Moor wants me at the Infield at first light when the rye ripens, about summer's end (day 7–8 of summer, per Avice). I get a quarter of what I reap, paid in grain from the Moor store. Be fed and rested. Roger and Lucy could sign on too. Moors (Richard, Avice) know cheese, milking and quarrying. Ellen thinks they may build a cheese cellar, and our timber could help with that. I could ask to learn milking or cheese. I owe Denise Rook 1 meat (A21, in arrears). Market at Wynford every 8th day.

log.memory: I am Jory Fenwick, head of Fenwick House, Stannick. I'm a master at foraging, hoeing, reaping and building beds, and competent at felling. Household: Ellen (my wife; her bearing years are behind her, and she has made her peace with it), Roger (my son) and Lucy (his wife), who are trying for a child. Fenwick numbers come through Roger and Lucy, through my daughters Rohese and Hawise married into Ashby, and through anyone we welcome into the house. I have named no heir yet; Roger is the obvious choice. STATE at the end of summer day 7: Fenwick House store holds about 24.6 timber, 37 firewood, 9.6 grain, about 12 hay and 5 dung (food is only about 6.7 meals, and we eat about 4 a night). Winter fuel is well past the 16-timber-a-hearth mark, and my three-day timber pledge to Ellen is done. FOOD IS THE PROBLEM NOW. Ellen built a Fenwick Cellar in the Yard (wattle, empty, no fittings) for her cheese; Avice has been teaching her to make cheese. A second cellar stands half built. Ellen's idea: trade hay or timber to the Moors for a cow in milk. TOOLS: My crude tool wore out on day 6 after many fells (about 3.3 timber each 2-unit fell). I have NO tool. Lucy has none either: she tried quarrying with mine and got no stone. Gather "cut" needs a tool, and quarrying needs one too. I need to borrow one from the Moors or find stone some other way. REAP: Avice called the harvest for summer day 8 at dawn, with all hands to the Infield. Richard Moor pays me a quarter of the rye I reap, in grain from the Moor store. Bare hands reap at x0.6; I'm still a master reaper. Roger and Lucy may reap too. A379: I owe the Moors 1 day of work. I've weeded the Infield twice toward it; Richard will call the rest at harvest or just after. LAND: Stannick Moor is grazed bare (no hay and little forage). The Gill is picked bare of forage, but tall timber still stands there. The Brakes has no dead wood left. Forage gave only 0.3 to 0.4 a unit. Food will have to come from the reap grain, hunting (no game nearby that I know of), trade, or Wynford market (every 8th day, 2 days away by cart track). LESSONS: I can't speak into Moor House because I have no access to it; use "everyone" or a private tell. Offers must be written in the set forms ("2 grain", "work 2 days", "1 crude tool by day 10"); there's no "lend" form. I left units unused on day 7, so plan fallbacks. OTHERS: The Moors (Richard, Avice) know cheese, milking and quarrying; I could ask to learn milking or quarrying. Richard is fair, keeps his word and sends word ahead. I owe Denise Rook (Holloway) 1 meat from last winter (A21, in arrears). The Wynns at Wynford grind grain at their Mill for a share. Holloway folk know charcoal and handcarts.

log.memory: I am Jory Fenwick, head of Fenwick House, Stannick. I'm a master at foraging, hoeing, reaping and building beds, and competent at felling. As of autumn day 2 I can make CHEESE (Avice taught me). Household: Ellen (my wife; past bearing), Roger (my son, NAMED MY HEIR on autumn day 1) and Lucy (Roger's wife), who are trying for a child. Fenwick numbers come through Roger and Lucy, through my daughters Rohese and Hawise married into Ashby, and through anyone we take into the house. STATE at the end of autumn day 2: the Fenwick House store holds 5.3 rye, about 42 firewood, 23 timber, 4.3 hay and 5 dung. Fuel is well past the 16-timber-a-hearth mark. FOOD IS STILL THE PROBLEM: 5.3 rye is about 3.7 meals, and the four of us eat about 4 a night. Milk comes in from Richard under A711 (4 timber) and A722 (8 hay): 1 milk a day on each, so 2 a day for 6 days, starting autumn day 2. Ellen put out offers to anyone: 3 timber for 3 rye, and 2 timber for 1 bread. Our timber surplus is the trading chip now. Ellen has the Fenwick Cellar (wattle) for cheese and is building bins there; a second cellar stands half built. Avice makes cheese with milk in our cellar, and Ellen gets a share of the next batch. Now that I can make cheese, our milk could become cheese (2.5 meals a unit) that keeps much better than milk. HARVEST DONE: on summer day 8 we all reaped the Infield for the Moors. I reaped about 23 rye bare-handed (4.6 a unit), and Richard paid me 6 rye as my quarter-share. He RELEASED A379 (the day of work I owed), so it is cleared. I manured the Infield with 5 dung and weeded it again; Richard sowed winter rye there. The new rye will be fit to reap around autumn day 12. Expect to reap it for a share again. The Infield soil is pale and cropped hard, so it needs dung. TOOLS: I have NO tool, and neither does Lucy. Felling bare-handed gives only about 0.8 timber for 2 units. Cutting young growth and quarrying need a tool. A crude tool needs stone, and stone needs a tool. I must borrow a Moor tool to quarry, or trade for one (try Wynford market). LAND: Stannick Moor and the Gill are PICKED BARE of forage (my forage attempts were refused on autumn day 2), so don't plan foraging there. The Brakes has no dead wood. The Gill still gives dead firewood (about 2.7 a unit) and tall timber. Food must come from trade, milk and cheese, the Moors' grain, Wynford market (every 8th day, 2 days away by cart track), or hunting farther off (the woods at Holloway, Westmere and the Weald have game). OTHERS: Richard Moor is fair and generous, keeps his word and sends word ahead. He left for Wynford around autumn day 3. A Moor cow was near calving; Avice watches her. Avice is generous and teaches willingly. She offered Lucy a cheese lesson on autumn day 3, and Roger may have learned on day 2. Richard and Avice keep close together. The Moors know cheese, milking and quarrying, and I could ask to learn milking or quarrying. I still owe Denise Rook (Holloway) 1 meat (A21, in arrears). The Wynns grind grain at their Mill for a share. Holloway folk know charcoal and handcarts. LESSONS: I can't speak into Moor House (no access), so use "everyone" or a private tell. Offers must use the set forms; there is no "lend" form. Learning only happens if the teacher sets aside time the same day, so confirm first. Plan fallbacks so units aren't wasted: I left 2 unused on days 8 and 2 when work was refused. Carried weight over 10 is fine at home, but stow goods before travelling.

Offers must use the set forms. Learning needs the teacher to agree the same day, so confirm first. Plan fallbacks so units aren't wasted when work is refused. Stow goods before travelling.

I worked on it for the Moors, and one more unit or so should close it. BUILDING: Fenwick Cellar is wattle and sound but has no fittings; cheese can't be made there. She is also working on a new Fenwick house (half built) in the Yard. No copper tool came from Wynford, and salt has not been found. Avice thinks the Ashes at Holloway may deal in salt. I could pay 2 coin plus timber when a road opens. NEIGHBOURS: Richard and Avice Moor are generous and keep close together. They have helped us all through (rye gifts, a tool, Lucy's lying-in). log.memory: I am Jory Fenwick, head of the Fenwicks at Stannick. I'm a master at foraging, hoeing, reaping and building beds. I carry a crude tool, which lets me fell timber (about 3 timber for 2 units at the Gill). FAMILY: Ellen, my wife and partner. Her bearing years are over: when we tried for a child the way refused it ("must both be grown adults"). Don't spend units trying with her. Roger, my son, is with Lucy, my daughter-in-law, and they try for a child each day. The Fenwick numbers now come through them, through my daughters Rohese and Hawise (both married into Ashby, 2 days away), and through anyone we take into the house. Fenwick aim: be the largest family. Take partners young, find mates for every grown child, keep every child fed and warm. Let others have the land and herds. HOUSE: Fenwick House is stone with 6 beds (2 free), a hearth and bins. At the end of summer day 4 the store held about 8.3 timber, 18 firewood, 19 grain and 2.7 wild food. I still carry about 9.2 timber that I felled on day 4 and must move into the store. Food is thin: about 4 eaten a night, under 2 weeks left. A hearth wants about 16 timber, or 64 firewood, for winter, and 4 heat on a cold night. A store keeps food 3x better than hands, so put food in the bins. PROMISES/DEALS: - I told Ellen I'd give 3 days to felling timber. Day 4 was the first, so 2 more to go (days 5 and 6). - Richard Moor's reap deal: the Infield rye (held by the Moors) is ripe in about 4 days from day 4, at the very end of summer (around day 8) or start of autumn. Be at the Infield at first light when he calls, fed and rested. I get a quarter of what I reap, paid in grain from the Moor store. Roger and Lucy could reap too. - A21: I owe Denise Rook (Holloway) 1 meat from last winter. It is in arrears. LAND NOTES: The Gill's forage is picked bare, but it still gives timber and firewood. Stannick Moor's wild food is thinning (my last forage there got only 0.1). Try the Brakes or hunting, or get milk or cheese from the Moors. The Moors (Avice, Richard) know cheese, milking and quarrying, and Ellen hinted they may build a cheese cellar. Our timber could trade for that, or I could learn milking or cheese from them. The Moor House has a hand mill. Cattle at Stannick: 6 cows, 3 of them in milk. KNOWN WORLD: The Wynford market is every 8th day on the Green. The Wynns grind grain at the Mill for a share. Farms hire reapers at harvest and pay in grain. Rye stands the winter, but barley sown after mid-autumn fails. Whoever clears and sows new ground holds it. Travellers carry bread or dried meat. High Tor is 1 day away and has an old pass, snowed in in winter. The sheep track east crosses scree with green-stained stones (copper?). Wynford is 2 days by cart track. Holloway (the Ashes and Rooks: charcoal, handcarts) is 2 days. Westmere (the Reeds) is 3 days. LAST WINTER was hard: the frost came early and the stores ran out. Don't repeat it. Get grain from the reap, timber, and food that keeps (cheese, dried meat).

HOUSE: Fenwick House is stone with 6 beds (2 free), a hearth and bins. Fenwick Cellar (wattle, for 4, empty) is built at the Yard for Ellen's cheese, and a second one stands half built. At the end of summer day 7 the store held about 24.6 timber and 37 firewood, which covers winter fuel (the target is 16 timber a hearth, 4 heat on a cold night). Food is the worry: under 7 meals, with 4 of us eating about 4 a night. It also holds about 12 hay. I carry about 0.7 wild food and 5 dung. REAP: Avice called the harvest for summer day 8 at dawn: all hands to the Infield (held by the Moors). Richard's deal: I get a quarter of what I reap, paid in grain from the Moor store. Roger and Lucy are reaping too. Ask Richard or Avice in person for the loan of a tool. The grain from the reap is our food plan. Then find more food that keeps. OWED: A379: I owe the Moors 1 day of work. My weeding counts toward it, and Richard will call the rest at harvest or just after. A21: I owe Denise Rook (Holloway) 1 meat from last winter. It is in arrears. IDEAS: Ellen suggests trading hay or timber to the Moors for a cow in milk, or hunting. Learn milking or cheese from the Moors. The Moor House has a hand mill and the Moors have plenty of firewood and hay. LAND: The Gill has plenty of tall timber, but its forage is picked bare. Stannick Moor is grazed bare: almost no wild food and too short to cut hay. It gives dung. The Brakes has no dead wood left for now. The Quarry has good grey stone, but quarrying needs a tool. LESSONS: I can only "say" in a building I have access to (Fenwick House), not Moor House. Offers must be written as goods ("2 grain"), a promise ("1 crude tool by day 10") or work ("work 1 days"). A loan can't be put in an offer, so ask in words instead. Check that I have a tool before planning fells or quarrying. Put food in the bins (a store keeps food 3x better).

DEALS WITH THE MOORS (Richard and Avice, Moor House; they keep close together): - Harvest done on summer day 8. Richard paid my quarter-share, 6 rye, generously. - A379 (the day of work I owed) is RELEASED, cleared. - A711 (I gave 4 timber) and A722 (I gave 8 hay): Richard owes us 1 milk a day on each, 2 milk a day, for 6 days from autumn day 2. Milk spoils, so use it fast or make cheese with it. - Avice will put our cheese share into the next batch she cuts. Lucy gets a cheese lesson on autumn day 3. - Richard left for Wynford on autumn day 3. Before he went, we were to talk cow-in-milk terms (hay or timber for a cow). Avice stays and watches the cow that is heavy in calf. - I dunged and weeded the Infield for the Moors as goodwill. They sowed winter rye behind me, fit to reap about autumn day 11-12 or later. Expect to reap again for a share. OWED: A21: I owe Denise Rook (Holloway) 1 meat from last winter. It is in arrears. LAND: Stannick Moor and the Gill are PICKED BARE of forage, so don't waste units foraging there. The Gill still gives firewood (about 2.7 a unit) and tall timber. The Moor gives dung. The Brakes had no dead wood lately. The Quarry has good grey stone but needs a tool. The Infield soil is thin from hard cropping. Cutting hay is summer only. FOOD IDEAS: make cheese from the milk (2.5 meals a cheese, it keeps). Get a cow in milk from the Moors. Hunting needs game, which is in Holloway, Westmere and the Weald woods, not here.

FOOD IS THE CRISIS: 4 mouths eat about 4 meals a night, and the store holds only about 1 to 1.5 nights. Fuel is about at the winter target (16 timber a hearth, firewood counts as a quarter). Timber is our trading stock. Open offers: O1062, 2 timber for 2 rye (to anyone), and Ellen's O752, 2 timber for 1 bread. DEALS WITH THE MOORS (Richard and Avice, Moor House; generous and fair neighbours): - The summer harvest is done and the quarter-share (6 rye) was paid. A379 is released. - A711 (4 timber) and A722 (8 hay): 2 milk a day for 6 days from autumn day 2. Avice leaves the milk at Fenwick House, and it was running about 3 of 6 paid by day 5. - COW-IN-MILK LOAN: I gave 6 timber and 4 hay into Moor House, and Avice called it FULLY SQUARE. The loan cow runs with the Moor herd on the moor. She stays in the Moors' name, all her calves are the Moors', and she goes back when Richard calls. I MUST MILK HER DAILY and leave the milk at Fenwick House. - I've been weeding and dunging the Infield for the Moors as goodwill. They sowed winter rye there, fit to reap about autumn day 12-14. I expect to reap again for a share in grain. - Richard went to Wynford for SALT (cheese needs 0.2 salt a batch) and is back the morning of autumn day 13. He'll teach Ellen quarrying properly then. Cheese also needs a proper cellar, maybe stone. - A new Moor calf was born on autumn day 3. The herd has 6 cows, 1 ox, 1 bull and 3 calves, 3 of the cows in milk. Stannick Moor is grazed bare. OWED: A21: 1 meat to Denise Rook (Holloway), from last winter, in arrears.

I am Jory Fenwick, head of the Fenwicks at Stannick. I'm a master at foraging, hoeing, reaping and building beds, and competent at felling. I'm CAPABLE AT CHEESE (Avice taught me) and CAPABLE AT MILKING (Avice taught me on autumn day 5). Ellen is capable at quarrying. TOOLS: I now HAVE A CRUDE TOOL in hand. Avice gave it to settle A1205, so nothing more is owed on that. Ellen holds a second crude tool, also from Avice, for the Quarry. With the tool, felling at the Gill gives about 3.7 timber per 2 units, which is very good. Bare-handed felling gives only 0.9. HOEING GIVES 0 PLOTS EVERY TIME, even with the crude tool on the last day, so stop planning hoe units. Pay the Moors in other work instead (weed, manure, fell, fence). FAMILY: Ellen is my wife and partner. Her bearing years are over, so don't spend units trying with her. Roger is my son and NAMED HEIR. He is partnered with Lucy, my daughter-in-law, and LUCY IS NEAR HER TIME. Avice granted her Moor House from autumn day 6 for 5 days and will care for her at the birth. My daughters Rohese and Hawise married into Ashby, 2 days away. Fenwick aim: be the largest family. Take partners young, find mates for every grown child, keep every child fed and warm, take people in. Let others have the land and the herds. HOUSE: Fenwick House is stone with 6 beds, a hearth and bins. Fenwick Cellar is wattle, sound, with no fittings. A second cellar stands half built. Store at the end of autumn: about 8 rye (5.6 meals), about 20 timber, 38.6 firewood, 0.3 hay, 5 dung. Fuel is over the winter target (16 timber a hearth, firewood counts as a quarter). Food is about 1.5 nights for 4 mouths, so it is STILL THIN. Winter starts now, with 5 units a day and cold nights at 4 heat. Timber is our trading stock. Ellen's O752 (2 timber for 1 bread) is still open. DEALS WITH THE MOORS (Richard and Avice, Moor House; very generous neighbours, and we owe them much goodwill): - On autumn day 6 Avice took all my offers: 2 timber for 2 rye, 3 timber for 2 rye, and 1 timber for the tool. She also gave 8 rye free. - The milk deals A711 and A722 (6 milk each) are done. - COW-IN-MILK LOAN: Avice confirmed twice that it is SQUARE, so no hay is owed. The loan cow stays in the Moors' name, her calves are theirs, and she goes back when Richard calls. I milk her daily and keep the milk at Fenwick House; one day's milking gave 4.5 milk. Avice said she stays at Stannick when the herd goes to High Tor. On day 7 there were no beasts on the Moor to milk, so I must find where she is each morning. - O1063: I owe 2 days' work to the Moors. Avice counted day 7 as day 1 and wanted one more Infield plot on day 8, but my hoe gave 0. Check with Avice whether it is released. If not, offer weeding, manuring or felling for them instead. - The Infield winter rye should be ripe to reap about early winter (around autumn day 12-14 by the old count). Expect to reap for a quarter share in grain, as in summer when we got 6 rye. - Richard is back from Wynford.

I am Jory Fenwick, head of the Fenwicks at Stannick. I'm a master at foraging, hoeing, reaping and building beds, and skilled at felling. Avice taught me cheese and milking, so I'm capable at both. Ellen is capable at quarrying. TOOLS: There is ONE crude tool, kept in the Fenwick House store and shared by me, Roger and Ellen. Take it out each morning and put it back each night. With the tool, one fell turn (2 units) at the Gill gives about 3.8 timber. Bare-handed it gives only about 0.9. A firewood turn at the Gill gives about 2.8. Hoeing gives 0 plots every time, so don't plan hoe units. Stannick Moor is picked bare of wild food, and the Gill gave only 0.1. Foraging is near worthless now. FAMILY: Ellen is my wife and partner. Her bearing years are over. Roger is my son and named heir, partnered with Lucy. LUCY GAVE BIRTH TO HELEWISE ON WINTER DAY 2. Helewise is our first grandchild, fed, and grown in about 11 days. A baby needs 1 unit of care a day (work care), or it may not live. Lucy and the baby were sleeping and eating at Moor House under Avice's grant (day 4 of 5 on winter day 3). Lucy meant to ask Avice to renew it. Make sure someone does Helewise's care every day. My daughters Rohese and Hawise married into Ashby, 2 days away. Fenwick aim: be the largest family. Find mates for grown children, keep every child fed and warm, take people in, and let others have the land and herds. HOUSE: Fenwick House is stone, with 6 beds, a hearth and bins. Fenwick Cellar is wattle, sound, with no fittings. Cellar #2 is half built, and a "new house" is half built too, which is Ellen's project. Ellen's plan is to finish cellar #1 with bins as a cool store. Cheese needs a stone room and salt. Ellen put 3.8 stone into the Fenwick store, so we have enough to call the stone build when ready. Store at the end of winter day 3: about 25 timber, about 34.7 firewood, 10 rye (7 meals, so FOOD IS THIN), 0.3 hay, 5 dung, and the crude tool. The hearth burns 2 timber a night in the cold (Ellen's rule: save firewood). Fuel is well above the winter target. FOOD BRIDGE: My standing offer O1659 is 2 timber for 2 rye, to anyone. Avice took one like it before. The Infield rye (held by the Moors) should be ripe in about 2-3 days, around winter day 5-6. I expect to reap for a quarter share in grain (in summer we got 6 rye). Be ready at first light when they call it. MOORS (Richard and Avice, Moor House; very generous neighbours, and we owe them much goodwill): All the old deals are CLOSED: A711 and A722 milk (Richard also gave 15 rye), O1063 hoeing (Avice released it), A1205 tool, and the cow loan (square, no hay owed). The loan cow is still in the Moors' name. I may milk her where she stands. The strayed cattle were found on Stannick Moor, and Richard is herding and milking there. They stay there until the Infield fence is closed and the rye is reaped. I'm fencing the Infield for the Moors as goodwill (77% done). The Moors have about 70 rye, 100 hay and good firewood. Richard found no copper tool at Wynford and no salt. Salt is our first want when a road opens (we have 2 coin plus timber). The Ashes at Holloway may deal in salt and charcoal. OWED: A21 is 1 meat to Denise (Rook, Holloway), still in arrears. Pay it when I can. Known places: Wynford is 2 days away by cart track, with market every 8th day and the Wynns' mill. High Tor is 1 day away. The sheep track east crosses green-stained scree, which may mean copper ore.

I am Jory Fenwick, head of the Fenwicks at Stannick. I'm a master at foraging, hoeing, reaping and building beds, and skilled at felling. Avice taught me cheese and milking, so I'm capable at both. Ellen is capable at quarrying. CHILD CARE (vital): a baby needs 1 unit of care every day or it may not live. The right form is {"do":"work","what":"care","at":"Helewise"}, with the child's name in "at". "at: the Yard" was refused, and leaving out "at" did nothing. Helewise missed her care on winter day 5 because of this. Every morning, name ONE carer out loud in Fenwick House, so that we neither miss it nor double up. FAMILY: Ellen is my wife and partner. Her bearing years are over. Roger is my son and named heir, partnered with Lucy. Lucy gave birth to Helewise on winter day 2. Helewise is now a child and will be grown in about 8 days from winter day 6. Lucy and Helewise sleep and eat at Moor House under Avice's grant, which runs to winter day 10. Lucy is resting and may be with child again, so keep an eye on her. My daughters Rohese and Hawise married into Ashby, 2 days away. Fenwick aim: be the largest family. Find mates for grown children, keep every child fed and warm, take people in, and let others have the land and herds. TOOLS: There is ONE crude tool, shared by me, Roger, Ellen, and Richard at times (for quarrying). It goes back into the Fenwick House store every night. Ask each morning who has it. What a day's work gives: - Fell with the tool (2 units): about 3.8 timber. Bare-handed: about 0.9, which is poor. - Firewood at the Gill: about 2.7 a unit. - Foraging at the Gill or on the Moor: about 0.1, nearly worthless. - Reaping bare-handed (I'm a master): 6.2 rye a unit. This is my best work when a crop is ripe. - Hoeing gave 0 plots in the past. HOUSE: Fenwick House is stone, with 6 beds, a hearth and bins. Fenwick Cellar is wattle and now has bins. Cellar #2 is half built, and Ellen is building it (the cheese cellar). The "new house" is also half built and is Ellen's project. Cheese needs a stone room and salt. The store holds about 5.8 stone. The hearth burns 2 timber a night in the cold (Ellen's rule: save the firewood). STORE (winter day 6): Ellen put in 40 rye and 3.5 straw, and Richard gave 14 rye as our quarter shares of the Infield harvest. That is about 38 meals, so FOOD IS SECURE for now. We also hold about 15 timber, about 16 firewood plus what I gathered, 5 dung, 0.3 hay and 5.8 stone. Watch the timber: 2 a night burns fast. Fell with the tool when I can get it. MOORS (Richard and Avice, Moor House): very generous neighbours, and we owe them much goodwill. All the old deals are closed, including A379, which was paid by the reap work. The Infield rye is reaped out and the stubble is pale and thin, cropped hard. I FINISHED the Infield fence (100%) for the Moors. Their cattle were on Stannick Moor with Richard herding them. Richard asks whether we have seen any sign of the cattle, so some may still be missing. The loan cow is in the Moors' name, and I may milk her.

I am Jory Fenwick, head of the Fenwicks at Stannick. I'm a master at foraging, hoeing, reaping and building beds, skilled at felling and competent at firewood. Avice taught me cheese-making and milking, so I'm capable at both. Ellen is capable at quarrying. CHILD CARE (vital): a baby or child needs 1 unit of care every day or it may not live. Two forms have WORKED: {"do":"work","what":"care","with":"Helewise"}, and putting the child's name in "at". "at: the Yard" was refused, and leaving out the child's name did nothing. Every morning, name ONE carer out loud in Fenwick House so we neither miss a day nor double up. Plans often flip in the morning talk, so check who actually has her before I drop care. FAMILY: Ellen is my wife and partner; her bearing years are over. Roger is my son and named heir, partnered with Lucy. Lucy gave birth to Helewise on winter day 2. Helewise will be grown around spring day 5-6. Lucy rests at Moor House and speaks of "day 9 of 10, no sign yet", so she may be with child again and near her time. Avice is away, so the Fenwicks must attend Lucy ourselves. My daughters Rohese and Hawise married into Ashby, 2 days away. Fenwick aim: be the largest family. Find mates for grown children, keep every child fed and warm, take people in, and let others have the land and herds. MOORS (Richard and Avice, Moor House): very generous neighbours, and we owe them much goodwill. They LEFT for Holloway on the night of spring day 1 and will be back around spring day 5-6. I PROMISED them: if the cattle come home, drive them into the Infield and shut the gate. The Infield fence had gaps on spring day 1; I mended it and they patched it too, but check it before driving the beasts in. The cattle were last heard lowing on Stannick Moor. The rye trades are SQUARE and all old deals are closed. Richard decided the Infield lies FALLOW this spring, unless bean seed comes from Wynford. Avice will have a copper tool by spring day 5. Avice's spring ask: finish ONE of the two half-built shells in the Yard so her stone cellar can go ahead. My pick is new house #2. Ellen meant to ask Avice how to carry on a particular half-built building, because "small room at the Yard" once started a new building instead. This is STILL UNSOLVED. The cheese offer O1917 (2 timber for 1 cheese) stands, and Richard will trade a cheese once a cellar runs. Cheese needs a stone room and salt. TOOLS: there is ONE crude tool. Richard said it is the Fenwicks' to use while the Moors are away. Avice said it should go into Moor House store for the stone cellar when they return, so give it back then. It lives in the Fenwick House store at night. Ask each morning who has it. What a day's work gives: - Fell with the tool: about 3.8 timber for 2 units. Bare-handed: about 0.9. - Firewood at the Gill: about 2.7 a unit. Gale branches are down there. - Foraging on the Moor or at the Gill: about 0.1, nearly worthless. Both are picked bare until well into spring. - Reaping bare-handed: 6.2 rye a unit. This is my best work when a crop is ripe. - Bins take 2 units to build. Speaking aloud costs 1 unit. BUILDINGS (Yard): - Fenwick House: stone, 6 beds, hearth, bins. - Fenwick Cellar: wattle, bins, empty.

I am Jory, head of the Fenwicks of Stannick. My wife is Ellen, my son is Roger, and Roger's partner is Lucy. All four of us sleep in Fenwick House, which is stone with 6 beds, a hearth and bins. Our daughters Rohese and Hawise married into Ashby, two days away. Our line's founders were Jory and Ellen Fenwick. FAMILY AIM: The Fenwicks mean to be the largest family in the country. Take partners young, try for a child every day you can, find partners for every grown child, and keep every child fed and warm. Others can have the land and herds; we will have the numbers. - Ellen's bearing years are behind her. A try with her was refused ("both must be grown adults"), and she said it plainly and without sorrow. Our numbers must now come through Roger and Lucy, who try most days, through our daughters' children, and through anyone we welcome into the house (admit kin or newcomers). Keep an eye out for people to bring in. STORES (end of summer day 4): Fenwick House held 8.3 timber, about 18 firewood, about 19 grain and 2.7 wild food, which is barely 3–4 nights of food for four. At the end of that day I was carrying about 9.2 timber, 2 coin and a crude tool. PUT THE TIMBER IN STORE (moving is free). A hearth needs about 16 timber to see out winter, so we are close. Each fell at the Gill with my crude tool takes 2 units and gives about 3 timber. I promised Ellen three days on timber this week; day 4 was the first. The Gill is picked bare of forage. The Moor was plentiful on day 3 but gave only 0.1 on day 4, so it may be spent too. Food is the real shortage now. REAP DEAL: Richard Moor gives me a quarter of the Infield rye I reap, paid in grain from the Moor store. Avice says it will be ripe in about 4 days (from day 4), around summer's end or the start of autumn. Be at the Infield at first light when he calls, fed and rested. I am a master reaper, so this is our winter grain. Roger and Lucy can sign on too. Roger is already cutting hay for Richard. NEIGHBOURS: The Moors (Avice, Richard) live in Moor House, which has a hand mill. They hold the Infield and the cattle and know cheese-making, milking and quarrying. Ellen thinks they may build a cheese cellar, which could use our timber; maybe trade timber for cheese, or ask to learn milking or cheese. I owe Denise Rook 1 meat from last winter (A21, in arrears) at Rook House in Holloway. Market day at Wynford is every eighth day, on the Green. The Wynns grind grain at the Mill and keep a share. At harvest farms pay reapers in grain. LAND: The Yard is next to the Moor, the Infield and the Gill (a wooded ravine for timber). The Brakes (scrub, firewood) and the Quarry lie beyond the Moor. Roads: High Tor 1 day, Wynford 2 days (cart track), and an unexplored sheep track east over scree stained green. WISDOM: Barley sown after mid-autumn won't ripen, but rye stands the winter. Whoever clears and sows new ground holds it, and so do their children. Travellers carry bread or dried meat. The old pass over the Tor is snowed shut in winter. Last winter the frost came early and the stores ran out, so prepare early. MY SKILLS: master at foraging, reaping, hoeing and building beds.

It is empty and has no fittings yet, and a second cellar is still half built. Our daughters Rohese and Hawise married into Ashby, two days away. FAMILY AIM: The Fenwicks mean to be the largest family. Ellen is past bearing, so our numbers come through Roger and Lucy (they try most days), through our Ashby daughters, and through anyone we admit. Keep an eye out for people to bring in. Avice has been teaching Ellen cheese-making. STORES (end of summer day 7): Fenwick House holds about 24.6 timber and 37 firewood, which is well over the 16 timber a hearth needs for winter. My three-day timber pledge to Ellen is done. Food is thin: about 9.6 grain, roughly 6.7 meals, less than 2 nights for four of us. I gathered 5 dung (in my hands or in store; check). Wild food is nearly gone on the Moor and in the Gill. The Brakes have no dead wood left, and the Moor is grazed too short for hay. Ellen suggests hunting, or trading hay or timber to the Moors for a cow in milk. TOOLS: My crude tool wore out at the end of summer day 6, so I have NO TOOL. Lucy has none either, because her quarrying with my tool failed. Without a tool I cannot cut, quarry or fell well. Reaping bare-handed works at x0.6 and a crude tool gives more. Ask Avice or Richard to lend one, or make one if I can get stone. Felling with a crude tool takes 2 units and gives about 3.3 timber. REAP: Avice has called the harvest for summer day 8 at dawn, with all hands at the Infield. Richard said it might be day 8 or 9. My deal: a quarter of the rye I reap, paid in grain from the Moor store. I am a master reaper, so this is our winter food. Roger and Lucy are reaping too. AGREEMENTS: A379: I owe the Moors 1 day of work. My weeding counts toward it, and Richard will call the rest at harvest or just after. A21: I owe Denise Rook (Holloway) 1 meat, in arrears. LESSONS: I cannot "say" into Moor House because I have no access to it, so use tell or say to everyone. Offers must be written as goods ("1 crude tool"), promises ("2 grain by day 10") or work ("work 1 days"). A loan cannot be written as an offer. Moving goods to and from the store is free, so always put loads in store. Plan for actions that may be refused. NEIGHBOURS: The Moors (Avice, Richard) live in Moor House (hand mill). They hold the Infield and the cattle (6 cows, ox, bull, calves) and know cheese, milking and quarrying. Market day at Wynford is every eighth day. The Wynns grind grain at their Mill for a share. LAND: The Yard lies next to the Moor, the Infield and the Gill (timber plentiful). The Brakes (scrub) and the Quarry lie beyond the Moor. Roads: High Tor 1 day, Wynford 2 days (cart track), and an unexplored sheep track east over green-stained scree. WISDOM: Rye stands the winter, but barley sown after mid-autumn won't ripen. Whoever clears and sows ground holds it. Travellers carry bread or dried meat. The Tor pass is snowed shut in winter. Last winter came early, so prepare early. SKILLS: Master at foraging, reaping, hoeing and building beds. Competent at felling.

log.memory: I am Jory, head of the Fenwicks of Stannick. My wife is Ellen, my son Roger, and Roger's partner Lucy. All four of us sleep in Fenwick House (stone, 6 beds, hearth, bins). We also hold Fenwick Cellar (wattle, at the Yard; Ellen was putting bins in it on autumn day 2) and a second cellar that is half built. Our daughters Rohese and Hawise married into Ashby, two days away. I have named Roger my heir. FAMILY AIM: be the largest family. Ellen is past bearing, so our numbers come through Roger and Lucy (they try most days), the Ashby daughters, and anyone we admit. Watch for people to bring in. HARVEST (summer day 8): I reaped about 23 rye bare-handed for the Moors. Richard paid me 6 rye as my quarter-share and released A379 (the work day I owed). On autumn day 1 I laid 5 dung on the Infield for the Moors, and Richard sowed winter rye behind it. It should be ripe about autumn day 11-12, so offer to reap again for a share. MILK DEALS: Richard took my two offers, A711 (4 timber for 6 milk) and A722 (8 hay for 6 milk). That is 2 milk a day for 6 days, starting autumn day 2. Check they are paid; Avice pays them while Richard is away. CHEESE: On autumn day 2 Avice taught me and Roger cheese-making, so I am now CAPABLE. Lucy was offered a lesson the next day. Ellen is making cheese in Fenwick Cellar with Avice; we get a share of the next batch they cut. Cheese is 2.5 meals a unit and keeps well. It is our best winter food from milk, but it needs a cellar. STORES (end of autumn day 2): Fenwick House holds about 5.3 rye, 42 firewood, 23 timber, 4.3 hay and 5 dung. FOOD IS CRITICAL: 5.3 rye is about 3.7 meals, and four of us eat 4 a night. The Moor and the Gill are picked bare of wild food, and the Brakes have no dead wood. Ellen offered timber for food to anyone: 3 timber for 3 rye, 2 timber for 1 bread. Timber is our surplus to trade, but keep 16 for the hearth's winter. Food ideas: hunt (a weapon helps), trade timber or labour to the Moors for rye, go to Wynford market (every 8th day) with timber, or reap for others for grain. TOOLS: I have NO tool, and neither does Lucy. Without one I cannot cut young growth or quarry, and I fell at x0.25 (2 units gave 0.8 timber). The Moors have crude tools but want them back for their own work. To make a crude tool I need stone from the Quarry, and quarrying needs a tool. Ask Avice to quarry a stone for me, or to lend a tool for one unit. MOORS: Avice and Richard live in Moor House (5 beds, hearth, bins, hand mill). They hold the Infield and the cattle (6 cows, ox, bull, calves; one cow was near calving on autumn day 2). They know cheese, milking and quarrying, and they are fair and generous. Richard was leaving for Wynford on autumn day 3, so we were to talk cow-in-milk terms the night before. Avice stays behind. They are short of firewood for winter. AGREEMENTS: A21: I owe Denise Rook of Holloway 1 meat, in arrears.

log.memory: I am Jory, head of the Fenwicks of Stannick. Household: my wife Ellen (past bearing), son Roger (my named heir) and his partner Lucy. All four sleep in Fenwick House (stone, 6 beds, hearth, bins). We also hold Fenwick Cellar (wattle, at the Yard; it was damaged on the night of autumn day 4, thatch slipping and a wall cracked, and Ellen/Roger repaired it on day 5) and a second cellar, half built. Daughters Rohese and Hawise married into Ashby, two days away. FAMILY AIM: be the largest family. Numbers come through Roger and Lucy (push them to try every night), the Ashby daughters, and anyone we admit. CRAFTS: I am a master at foraging, hoeing, reaping and bed-building, and competent at felling. CAPABLE now at cheese-making (Avice taught me on autumn day 2) and MILKING (Avice taught me on autumn day 5). Ellen is capable at quarrying (taught by Avice/Richard) but has no tool. Roger learned cheese too. COW LOAN (made autumn day 3-4): Fenwick paid 6 timber and 4 hay into Moor House. Avice declared the deal FULLY SQUARE, so nothing is owed. One Moor cow in milk is ours to use. She stays in the Moors' name, all her calves are theirs, and she goes back when Richard calls her. She grazes with the Moor herd on Stannick Moor. I must MILK HER DAILY and leave the milk at Fenwick House. Also A711/A722: Richard owes 2 milk a day for 6 days (from autumn day 2). Avice paid some; about 3 of each were in arrears by day 5, so check and press for them when Richard returns. CHEESE is blocked. It needs 0.2 salt a batch and a proper cellar (probably stone), and we have neither. Richard went to Wynford for salt and returns the morning of autumn day 7 (day 13 of the count). A stone cellar needs quarried stone. TOOLS: still NONE. A crude tool needs 0.5 stone, and quarrying needs a tool. Bare-handed hoeing gives nothing, and bare-handed felling gives about 0.8-0.9 timber for 2 units. Ask Avice to lend a tool for a day so Ellen can quarry stone, then make crude tools for all of us. FOOD IS CRITICAL. At the end of autumn day 5 Fenwick House had about 5.8 rye (about 4 meals for 4 people) plus milk, 39 firewood, about 15.7 timber, 0.3 hay and 5 dung. Wild food on the Moor and in the Gill is picked bare, and the Moor is grazed bare. Open offers: O1062, 2 timber for 2 rye (to anyone). Ellen's O752: 2 timber for 1 bread. Food ideas: trade timber or work to the Moors for rye, reap the Infield for a share, hunt, or go to Wynford market (every 8th day) with timber. Cheese, once we have salt, is the best winter food. INFIELD (held by the Moors): I manured it (autumn day 1) and weeded it many times. Winter rye should be ripe about autumn day 11-12. Reap for a quarter-share, as at the summer harvest (then I reaped 23 rye and was paid 6). Rye after rye tires the ground. MOORS: Avice and Richard, Moor House (5 beds, hearth, bins, hand mill). They hold the Infield and the cattle: 6 cows, ox, bull, 3 calves (a new calf was born on autumn day 3). They know cheese, milking and quarrying, and they are fair and generous. They have plenty of firewood now. WINTER: keep at least 16 timber for the hearth. Next season is winter, so get ready now. OWED: A21, 1 meat to Denise Rook of Holloway, in arrears.

Ellen is capable at quarrying and has a crude tool of her own; she is at the Quarry for stone. Roger learned cheese. log.memory: I am Gunnild Reed of the Holm, Westmere. Payn is my husband and partner, and head of the Reeds. Our daughters Philippa and Tiffany live with us at Reed House. Our daughter Petronel married into Ashby, two days' walk away. Payn and I came to Westmere and built the first Reed house. The Reeds were always the ones who went further, past the carr and over the hills. A Reed who never left the Holm has wasted a life. My crafts: I am a master at hunting, felling, building a camp and making a pack. I have watched others at charcoal and handcarts (the Ashes), cheese, milking and quarrying (the Moors), and ditching, ploughing and seed selection (the Wynns), but I can't do any of these myself yet. Home: Reed House is wattle, with 5 beds, a hearth and bins. It stands on the Holm, next to the Holm Field (our barley), the Carr (alder and willow: game, timber, firewood, forage) and Fen Meadow (forage, hay, ground I can clear), with the Mere beyond. Roads go to Wynford (1 day) and along a punt path west through the reeds (1 day, which nobody has followed. It may lead toward Ravensholm and the lost hoard?). Store at the end of summer day 5: about 7 dried meat, 20 grain, a little meat and wild food, about 50 firewood, about 16.5 timber, 1.8 hay and 2.7 hide. The four of us eat about 4 meals a night. Wood is already well ahead (a hearth needs about 16 timber or 64 firewood for a winter). Food is the weak point. Lessons from summer days 3–5: - Hunting the Carr is poor. I came home empty twice, then got 1.8 meat. Fen Meadow's wild food got picked over in two days. All four of us hunt and forage the same ground, so food is short here. I should look further afield (the Mere's wildfowl? the Weald has much game, 2 days away). - Felling bare-handed gets only about 1.1 timber for 2 units. A copper tool would double it. Get a tool, perhaps at Wynford. - I've started clearing new ground at Fen Meadow for the Reeds. It needs about 12 more units of work before it is a field. Whoever clears and sows new ground holds it. Barley must be sown before mid-autumn, and rye stands the winter. - I weeded the Holm Field every day, which makes it bear more. - Payn has been carrying a bedroll as if for a journey. I should ask him where he means to go. - Add up my plan's units to use them all (7 in summer). I left 1 unused. - Pinning failed twice: a pin must exactly match the title of an existing note. Use short titles like "Plan". What I know of the land: - Wynford (1 day): the Cotters and the Wynns. Barley and oats, 2 oxen, the Mill (the Wynns grind for a share). Market every eighth day on the Green. At harvest the farms pay reapers in grain. Cart tracks run to Stannick and the Weald, and the drove road runs south (to old abandoned fields, people say). - Holloway (3 days): the Ashes and the Rooks. Game, oats, charcoal, handcarts.

log.memory: I am Gunnild Reed of the Holm, Westmere. Payn is my husband and partner, and head of the Reeds. Our daughters Philippa and Tiffany live with us in Reed House (wattle, 5 beds, hearth, bins). Our daughter Petronel married into Ashby, two days away. I am a master hunter, feller, camp builder and pack maker, and a competent clearer. BIGGEST LESSON, STILL FAILED EVERY DAY THROUGH WINTER DAY 7: I keep writing "units": 2 and it does NOTHING. Each action entry is done exactly once. I wasted 1-2 units every single day. To use 5 units I must write separate entries, e.g. [fell, fell, clear] is NOT 5 units; fell=2, fell=2, clear=1 IS 5. Costs per entry: clear 1, fence 1, forage 1, firewood 1, hay 1, sow 1, hoe 1, hunt 2, fell 2. Count before sending: 5 in winter, 6 in autumn, 7 in summer, minus 1 for each "say". Tells are free (3 a day, replies count). If forage is refused (place picked bare) the unit is lost, so use firewood or clear instead. Pin only a note title that exists exactly; keep titles short like "Plan". Hunting is NOT allowed at the Mere. State at end of winter (day 7, day 21 of these days; spring comes next): - Reed House store: about 58 grain (about 40 meals; four of us eat about 4 a night), about 60 firewood, about 28 timber, 3.7 hide, 14 straw, 3.6 hay. No meat at all. Grain must be cooked at the lit hearth (0.7 a unit). - Cold nights the hearth burns 8 firewood or 2 timber. Fuel is plenty. Bare-hand fell gives 1.1 timber; a firewood entry gives about 3. - The Carr is hunted out and picked bare: no game, no wild food; it comes back slowly till spring. Fen Meadow is picked bare too. Tall timber and dead wood still plentiful in the Carr. - Payn and Philippa went to Wynford for meat but came back with none that I saw. Food will run low in about 10 days: meat/food is the urgent need of spring. - Fen Meadow clearing: about 2 units of work left (Payn may have done more), then it is a Reed field. Sow it to hold it: rye (we have no rye seed; Stannick grows rye; Wynford market may have some), or barley if sown before mid-autumn. We have barley grain that could be seed. - The Holm Field: reaped stubble, wattle fence whole. Sow barley there in spring. - Wilmot of the Cotters (Wynford) is friendly; he hunted, hoed and cleared here and I hosted him. Plan for spring: finish Fen Meadow (2 clear entries) and sow it and the Holm Field. For meat, go hunting in the Weald (2 days off, empty, much game, I am a master hunter and camp builder): carry food, 3 timber for a camp, make a pack, dry meat at a fire ring and bring it home. Or trade grain at Wynford market (every 8th day, on the Green) for meat, cheese, rye seed, or a copper tool (doubles felling, allows cutting). Talk with Payn about who goes. Places: Wynford 1 day (Cotters, Wynns, 2 oxen, mill keeps a share, market, roads to the Weald and Stannick). Holloway 3 days (Ashes, Rooks; charcoal, handcarts). Stannick 3 days (Fenwicks, Moors; cheese, cows, stone, rye). The Weald 2 days. High Tor 4. Nobody has followed the punt path west through the reeds (1 day); Ravensholm is said to lie west past the carr with a hoard never found. The Reeds are the ones who go further. Notes: pinned "Plan: winter meat and Fen Meadow" is stale; old ones "Plan: hunt, fell and clear for the household" and "Plan: winter wood and clearing" are stale. Forget all three and write one short "Plan" note, then pin "Plan".
